hints.title: Split at the sign change
hints.body: Write the left side separately for negative and nonnegative inputs. This gives a quadratic equation on each half-axis. Keep the half-axis condition beside each equation.
hints.recap: An absolute-value equation can have different algebraic branches on opposite sides of zero.
hints.pitfall: A root of a branch equation counts only if it lies in that branch.
hints.pause: Derive the two quadratic equations and state where each one is allowed.

recall.reminder: An absolute-value equation can have different algebraic branches on opposite sides of zero.

hints.title: Use root signs as well as discriminants
hints.body: Treat positive, negative and zero values of the intercept parameter separately. A quadratic with negative root product has two real roots of opposite signs. Use this fact to constrain one half-axis before considering the other.
hints.recap: The product of the roots can determine their signs without requiring their exact values.
hints.pitfall: Adding the two unrestricted quadratic root counts can overcount roots outside the branches and can count zero twice.
hints.pause: For each intercept case, bound the number of admissible roots on each half-axis.

recall.reminder: The product of the roots can determine their signs without requiring their exact values.

hints.title: Prove the possibilities are achievable
hints.body: A bound alone does not establish the complete list. Sketch the piecewise curve against suitable lines and choose parameter values that attain each count you think is possible. Check tangent contacts and the origin explicitly.
hints.recap: To prove an exact list of possible values, rule out other values and exhibit each value in the list.
hints.pitfall: A tangency is one distinct root even though its quadratic root is repeated.
hints.pause: Produce examples, verify their roots in the original equation and finish the complete root-count list.

recall.reminder: To prove an exact list of possible values, rule out other values and exhibit each value in the list.

solution:
1. Split the equation. For x≥0, it becomes x2−px−q=0. For x<0, it becomes x2+px+q=0. Only roots in the stated half-axis are admissible.

2. Bound the counts when q≠0. If q>0, the first quadratic has root product −q<0, so it has exactly one positive root. The negative branch has at most two roots, giving at least one and at most three in total. If q<0, the negative-branch quadratic has product q<0, so it has exactly one negative root, while the positive branch has at most two. The same total bounds follow.

3. Handle the origin separately. When q=0, factor the original equation as x(|x|−p)=0. If p>0, its distinct roots are −p,0,p; if p≤0, only 0 is possible. Thus there are never zero or four roots.

4. Attain every intermediate possibility. With (p,q)=(0,0), only x=0 solves the equation. With (p,q)=(2,1), the negative branch is (x+1)2=0 and the positive branch has admissible root 1+2, giving two distinct roots. With (p,q)=(1,0), the roots are −1,0,1, giving three.

Answer E: the complete list is 1,2,3.
knowledgePattern: Bound and attain distinct root counts by splitting an absolute-value equation at zero
